title: UNIT 4: DETERMINANTS AND THEIR PROPERTIES
notes:
✓ Determinant → a number associated with a square matrix.

Determinants are used to:
◆ determine whether a matrix is invertible
◆ find inverses of square matrices
◆ solve systems of linear equations
◆ solve problems involving areas, interpolation and collinearity.

title: 4.1  DETERMINANT OF A 2 × 2 MATRIX
notes:
For a square matrix:

A = [ a  b ]
       [ c  d ]

✓ Determinant:
|A| = ad − bc

Example:
A = [ 2  3 ]
       [ 1  4 ]

|A| = (2)(4) − (3)(1)
    = 8 − 3
    = 5.

→ A determinant is a number, not another matrix.

title: DETERMINANT AND INVERTIBILITY
notes:
For a square matrix A:

◆ If |A| ≠ 0 → A is invertible (non-singular).

◆ If |A| = 0 → A is singular and has no inverse.

Example:
A = [ 2  4 ]
       [ 1  2 ]

|A| = (2)(2) − (4)(1) = 0.

Therefore, A is singular and A⁻¹ does not exist.

→ The determinant is therefore an important test for invertibility.

title: 4.2  MINORS OF MATRIX ELEMENTS
notes:
✓ Minor of an element → the determinant obtained after deleting the row and column containing that element.

For a₍ᵢⱼ₎, its minor is denoted by Mᵢⱼ.

Example:
A = [ 1  2  3 ]
       [ 4  5  6 ]
       [ 7  8  9 ]

To find M₁₂, delete row 1 and column 2:

[ 4  6 ]
[ 7  9 ]

Therefore:
M₁₂ = (4)(9) − (6)(7) = −6.

→ Minor → delete the corresponding row and column, then take the determinant.

title: COFACTORS OF MATRIX ELEMENTS
notes:
✓ Cofactor of a₍ᵢⱼ₎ → its minor multiplied by the appropriate sign.

Formula:
Cᵢⱼ = (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ Mᵢⱼ

Sign pattern:

[ +  −  + ]
[ −  +  − ]
[ +  −  + ]

Example:
If M₁₂ = −6,
then:
C₁₂ = (−1)¹⁺²(−6)
     = (−1)(−6)
     = 6.

→ Minor gives the value; cofactor gives the value with its correct sign.

title: 4.3  DETERMINANT OF A 3 × 3 MATRIX
notes:
For:
A = [ a₁₁  a₁₂  a₁₃ ]
       [ a₂₁  a₂₂  a₂₃ ]
       [ a₃₁  a₃₂  a₃₃ ]

✓ The determinant can be found by cofactor expansion along any row.

Expanding along the first row:
|A| = a₁₁C₁₁ + a₁₂C₁₂ + a₁₃C₁₃

Example:
A = [ 1  2  3 ]
       [ 0  4  5 ]
       [ 1  0  6 ]

|A| = 1(24) − 2(−5) + 3(−4)
    = 24 + 10 − 12
    = 22.

title: COFACTOR EXPANSION
notes:
✓ The determinant of a 3 × 3 matrix can be expanded along any row or column.

For a row:
|A| = aᵢ₁Cᵢ₁ + aᵢ₂Cᵢ₂ + aᵢ₃Cᵢ₃

→ Best strategy → choose the row or column containing the most zeros.

Example:
A = [ 2  0  0 ]
       [ 3  4  5 ]
       [ 1  6  7 ]

Expanding along the first row is easiest because it contains two zeros.

For a triangular matrix:
|A| = product of the main diagonal entries.

title: 4.4  IMPORTANT PROPERTIES OF DETERMINANTS
notes:
◆ Interchanging two rows changes the sign:
|B| = −|A|.

◆ Multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k:
|B| = k|A|.

◆ Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant.

Example:
R₂ → R₂ + 3R₁
Determinant remains unchanged.

◆ For a triangular matrix:
|A| = product of diagonal entries.

◆ Transpose:
|Aᵀ| = |A|.

◆ Product:
|AB| = |A||B|.

title: USING ROW OPERATIONS TO FIND DETERMINANTS
notes:
✓ Row operations can simplify a determinant before calculating it.

Example strategy:
1. Transform the matrix into triangular form.
2. Track any row swaps or row scaling.
3. Multiply the diagonal entries.
4. Adjust the result according to the row operations used.

◆ Adding a multiple of one row to another → determinant unchanged.

◆ Swapping two rows → change the sign.

◆ Multiplying a row by k → multiply determinant by k.

→ This method is especially useful for larger determinants.

title: 4.5  INVERSE USING ADJOINT AND DETERMINANT
notes:
For an invertible square matrix A:

✓ A⁻¹ = 1/|A| Adj(A)

where Adj(A) → adjoint of A, obtained from the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

Procedure:
1. Find all minors.
2. Convert minors to cofactors.
3. Form the cofactor matrix.
4. Transpose it to obtain Adj(A).
5. Calculate |A|.
6. Use A⁻¹ = Adj(A)/|A|.

→ This formula is valid only when |A| ≠ 0.

title: 4.6  CRAMER'S RULE
notes:
✓ Cramer's Rule → uses determinants to solve a system of linear equations when the coefficient matrix is invertible.

For AX = B:

D = |A|

For two variables:

x = Dₓ/D

y = Dᵧ/D

where Dₓ is obtained by replacing the x-column of A with the constants, and Dᵧ by replacing the y-column.

Example:
x + y = 5
2x − y = 1

D = | 1   1 |
       | 2  −1 | = −3

Dₓ = | 5   1 |
        | 1  −1 | = −6

Dᵧ = | 1   5 |
        | 2   1 | = −9

Therefore:
x = 2,
y = 3.

title: NO SOLUTION OR INFINITELY MANY SOLUTIONS
notes:
If the determinant of the coefficient matrix is zero:

|A| = 0

→ Cramer's Rule cannot be used to obtain a unique solution.

The system may have:

◆ No solution → equations are inconsistent.

Example:
x + y = 3
x + y = 5

Subtracting gives:
0 = 2

◆ Infinitely many solutions → equations are dependent and at least one variable is free.

→ Therefore, when |A| = 0, use elimination or another method to determine the type of solution.

title: 4.7  APPLICATIONS OF DETERMINANTS
notes:
✓ Determinants have several important applications.

◆ Polynomial interpolation → finding a polynomial that fits given data points and estimating unknown values.

◆ Area of a triangle → determinants can calculate the area of a triangle in the xy-plane.

For points (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃):

Area = 1/2 | x₁(y₂−y₃) + x₂(y₃−y₁) + x₃(y₁−y₂) |

◆ Collinearity → three points are collinear when the corresponding determinant is zero.

◆ Equation of a line → determinants can be used to find the equation of a line passing through two points.

title: UNIT 4 KEY FORMULAS & QUICK REVISION
notes:
◆ 2 × 2 determinant:
|A| = ad − bc

◆ Minor:
Mᵢⱼ = determinant after deleting row i and column j.

◆ Cofactor:
Cᵢⱼ = (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲMᵢⱼ.

◆ 3 × 3 determinant:
|A| = ΣaᵢⱼCᵢⱼ along any row or column.

◆ Triangular matrix:
|A| = product of diagonal entries.

◆ Transpose:
|Aᵀ| = |A|.

◆ Product:
|AB| = |A||B|.

◆ Invertibility:
|A| ≠ 0 → A is invertible.

|A| = 0 → A is singular.

◆ Inverse:
A⁻¹ = Adj(A)/|A|.

◆ Cramer's Rule:
x = Dₓ/D,
y = Dᵧ/D.

✓ Main idea → determinants connect matrices, inverses, systems of equations and geometric applications.
